name: Appajim
title: Descendant of Jerahmeel in the tribe of Judah
summary: Appajim belonged to Jerahmeel's branch of the tribe of Judah and is known from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles. As the son of Nadab and father of Ishi, he formed an important link in this family line. Because his brother Seled died childless, it was Appajim who alone continued Nadab's branch. The genealogy he is part of was recorded to keep track of Judah's family lines and ensure documentation of tribal affiliation and inheritance rights in Israel's history.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Jerahmeel's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Appajim is recorded as the son of Nadab and brother of Seled in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's descendants. Seled died without children, while Appajim carried on the family line.

keyEvents.title: Father of Ishi
keyEvents.description: Appajim became the father of Ishi, who continued Jerahmeel's family line through subsequent generations.

keyEvents.title: Part of Judah's tribal lineage
keyEvents.description: Appajim's lineage is part of the larger genealogy of the tribe of Judah, which documents Israel's tribal history from Judah through Jerahmeel's branch.

versions.summary: Appajim was a descendant of Judah through the lineage of Jerahmeel. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as the son of Nadab and the father of Jishai. His significance lies in his place in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.
versions.title: Descendant of Jerahmeel
versions.reason: [minor] Appajim belongs to a genealogy that traces back to the tribe of Judah. The exact time period is unknown, but 'united-kingdom' is a reasonable placement based on the fact that Jerahmeel's lineage likely extends to this period. Alternatively, 'patriarchs' or 'judges' could have been relevant, but we leave this as it is.; [minor] The role 'patriarch' is somewhat misleading for someone primarily known from a genealogy without any leadership role. A more precise term would be 'forefather' or 'ancestral link'. 'Patriarch' is usually used of the great forefathers (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob).; [minor] The four key events largely overlap and cover the same information. Event 1 and 2 both concern 1 Chron 2:30-31. Consider merging them into fewer, more concise events.; [minor] There are no footnotes that could provide linguistic background for the name Appajim or context about Jerahmeel's lineage.

versions.summary: Appajim was a descendant of Judah through the lineage of Jerahmeel. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as the son of Nadab and the father of Jishai. His brother Seled died without descendants, which gave Appajim an important role as the one who carried forward Nadab's branch of Jerahmeel's family. His significance lies in his place in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, which was recorded to document Israel's tribal history.
versions.title: Descendant of Jerahmeel in the tribe of Judah
versions.reason: [major] Appajim is a person primarily known from the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, and his placement in Jerahmeel's lineage places him chronologically closer to the time of the patriarchs or judges than to the united monarchy. The genealogical records span many generations, and Appajim likely lived in an earlier era. 'Patriarchs' or 'judges' would have been more precise, but since the exact time period is uncertain and he is several generations after Judah, 'judges' is a reasonable choice.; [minor] The summary closely resembles version 1. It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from the previous version and provide a fresher perspective.; [minor] The third key event ('Part of the tribe of Judah's lineage') contains many verses and serves more as general contextualization than a specific event tied to Appajim. It could be tightened to include only the most relevant verses.

footnotes.text: The name Appajim (Hebrew: אַפַּיִם, ʾAppayim) likely means 'nostrils' or 'face', derived from the Hebrew word 'af' (אַף) meaning 'nose'. The dual form may suggest 'two nostrils' or be used as a personal name with an intensified meaning.

Jerahmeel's lineage in 1 Chronicles 2 is part of the extensive genealogies in the books of Chronicles that served to legitimize tribal affiliation and inheritance rights after the exile. These lists were important for restoring social and religious order following the return from Babylon.

Seled, Appajim's brother, is mentioned as childless (1 Chron 2:30). In the biblical context, dying without descendants was a serious loss, as it meant one's name would not be carried forward in Israel. Appajim thus took on a more important role as the one who continued Nadab's lineage.

The Jerahmeelites are mentioned several times in the Old Testament as a clan in the Negev region, associated with the tribe of Judah. David had contact with the Jerahmeelites during his time as a fugitive in the Negev (1 Sam 27:10; 30:29), which shows the clan's geographical and political ties to southern Judah.
